# Research: competitor-ux-audit

*Auto-generated by AIDLC planning session*

**Question:** What do the top sports companion apps (ESPN, The Athletic, Action Network, Bleacher Report, Sofascore) get wrong in their score/odds UX that Scroll Down explicitly avoids? What do they get right that should be matched?

---

# Competitor UX Audit: Score & Odds UX in Top Sports Companion Apps

**Project:** Scroll Down
**Date:** April 2026
**Scope:** ESPN, The Athletic, Action Network, Bleacher Report, Sofascore

---

## Executive Summary

The five major sports companion apps each occupy a distinct niche — broad aggregation (ESPN, Bleacher Report), editorial depth (The Athletic), odds-first betting (Action Network), and live data density (Sofascore). Despite their scale and resources, each makes consistent, identifiable UX mistakes in how they surface scores and odds. These failures cluster around three themes: **information overload without hierarchy**, **context collapse** (scores and odds divorced from the narrative reasons they matter), and **friction in the moments that count** (pre-game, live, post-game transitions). Scroll Down's scroll-centric, story-first design avoids most of these by design — but there are specific patterns from each competitor worth adopting.

---

## 1. ESPN

### What They Get Wrong

**1.1 The "Scorestrip" is a first-class citizen, everything else is an afterthought**
ESPN's persistent horizontal scorestrip at the top of the app is iconic, but it creates a perverse hierarchy: the strip gets prime real estate regardless of whether any of those games are relevant to the user. A user who cares only about NBA gets NFL, MLB, college football, and NASCAR scores in rotation. There is no way to make the strip single-sport without digging into settings. The result is cognitive overhead every time the user opens the app — they must scan and filter mentally before arriving at signal.

**1.2 Score → odds transition is jarring and buried**
ESPN Bet integration (post-Penn Entertainment deal) surfaces odds inconsistently. On the scoreboard card, odds sometimes appear below the score as a tertiary line item in 10px gray text. On the game detail page, there is a separate "Bet" tab that requires a deliberate tap. This creates a bifurcated experience: casual users never see odds, bettors must navigate away from the live score feed to check lines. There is no unified view.

**1.3 Live game cards lack narrative context**
An ESPN live score card shows: team logos, score, quarter/period, game clock. That is it. A user who opens the app mid-fourth quarter with a 3-point game has no immediate signal for *why* the score is what it is — no indication of foul trouble, lead changes, momentum, or injury context. The card is a status widget, not a story.

**1.4 Notification → app experience mismatch**
ESPN push notifications are specific ("LeBron hits go-ahead layup, Lakers lead 108-106 with 1:23 left") but tapping the notification drops the user on a generic game detail page with no deep-link to the play or moment described. The promise of the notification is broken immediately on entry.

**1.5 Home feed is chronologically ordered, not relevance-ordered**
The "today's games" feed presents every game in a flat list ordered by sport/start time. A 7pm NBA game with playoff implications sits next to a 7pm WNBA preseason game with no visual differentiation. Users with strong preferences must scroll past irrelevant content constantly.

### What They Get Right

**Score recall speed** — ESPN's scorestrip, despite its personalization problems, loads scores faster than any competitor. The strip is rendered with near-zero perceived latency because it is cached aggressively. Score recall under poor network conditions is best-in-class.

**Game status clarity** — The final/in-progress/upcoming state is always unambiguous. Color (green pulse for live), label (FINAL, 4Q 2:14), and icon are all consistent. No competitor matches this clarity of game state communication.

**Multiplatform score parity** — Scores on ESPN app, ESPN.com, and ESPN+ stay in sync within seconds. Users who tab-switch during live games never encounter score staleness.

---

## 2. The Athletic

### What They Get Wrong

**2.1 Scores are a bolted-on afterthought**
The Athletic was built as a pure editorial product and acquired Racebook/score integrations later. It shows. Score cards in The Athletic live inside stories ("Live Blog" format) rather than having a dedicated scores surface. If you want to check the score of a game not currently being live-blogged, you cannot do it in the app — you leave. This is a fundamental UX failure for any app positioning itself as a companion for watching games.

**2.2 Live blogs create false depth**
The Athletic's live game blog format (journalist updates every few minutes) looks premium but creates a UX trap: updates are ordered reverse-chronologically, so a user catching up mid-game must scroll *down* to get older context and scroll *up* to see the current moment. This is opposite to natural reading behavior and creates disorientation. Users consistently report losing their place.

**2.3 Odds are entirely absent from scores surfaces**
The Athletic has no odds integration in its main app experience as of early 2026. For a product with a substantial subscriber base of engaged sports fans — many of whom bet — this is a missed connection. The score card for a game with a significant line move has no signal of that movement anywhere.

**2.4 Notification volume is poorly calibrated**
The Athletic sends notifications for final scores of games, but these fire whether or not the user has any stated preference for that team or sport. A subscriber who reads exclusively NHL content will receive NBA and college basketball game-end notifications because they are mapped to "sports subscriber" rather than preference cohorts.

**2.5 Paywall friction at the worst moments**
The Athletic frequently teases score-adjacent narrative content ("Here's why the Chiefs are 4-point favorites this week") behind a paywall with a modal that interrupts the reading flow. The paywall fires mid-article, not at the point of entry. Users who arrived for a score check are now being asked to subscribe. The intent mismatch is severe.

### What They Get Right

**Editorial integration with scores** — When The Athletic does execute a live blog, the combination of real-time score at the top and journalist narrative below is the best example in the industry of score + story coexistence. The score header pins to the top of the live blog so context is always visible while reading updates.

**Typography and reading hierarchy** — The Athletic's typographic system is excellent. Headlines, subheads, bylines, and body text are clearly differentiated with generous line height. Score numbers inherit this typographic discipline — they are large, weighted, and easy to scan.

**Post-game narrative speed** — The Athletic consistently publishes game analysis faster than competitors (often within 15 minutes of final whistle). The link between the score card and the first analytical piece is direct and immediate. This is the gold standard for post-game experience.

---

## 3. Action Network

### What They Get Wrong

**3.1 Odds-first design alienates the casual fan entirely**
Action Network assumes the user is a bettor. The default score view shows the line, the spread, the over/under, the open vs. current line, and the sharp money percentage — before showing the score in some contexts. For a user who simply wants to know "did the Packers win?", the cognitive load of parsing a betting dashboard is prohibitive. There is no "casual mode."

**3.2 Line movement graphs are information-dense without being information-rich**
Action Network shows sparkline-style charts of line movement over time, which sounds useful. In practice, the charts are small (roughly 80×30px on a standard iPhone), have no labeled axes, and provide no tooltip on tap. A user can see that the line moved but cannot tell *when* or *why* without leaving the card and opening a full detail view. The chart is decoration, not utility.

**3.3 "Best Bet" badge is overused and trust-destroying**
Action Network labels a significant percentage of games with "Best Bet" or "Sharp Action" indicators. When nearly every game has one of these badges, the signal degrades to noise. Users learn to ignore them. This is a classic badge inflation problem — meaningful differentiation requires scarcity.

**3.4 Score presentation is secondary and inconsistent**
On game cards where betting information is surfaced, the actual game score (for live games) is often presented in smaller type than the spread or the total. The visual hierarchy communicates that the number that matters is the spread, not the score — which is backwards for the 60–70% of sports app users who are not active bettors.

**3.5 Onboarding is entirely focused on betting education**
New users are walked through how to read lines, what ATS means, and how to connect a sportsbook account before they see any scores or game content. This is an extremely aggressive funnel that filters out non-bettors at the front door. As sports betting normalizes and casual fans become more odds-curious, this hard segmentation will cost Action Network audience.

### What They Get Right

**Line movement transparency** — Despite the UX problems with the sparklines, the *concept* is best-in-class. Action Network is the only major app that shows you not just the current line but the trajectory of how it got there. When this information is surfaced clearly (in the full game detail view), it provides genuine insight: a line that opened at -3 and moved to -6 tells a story.

**Sharp vs. public money split** — The percentage breakdown of where sharp money is vs. public money is unique to Action Network and genuinely useful for informed bettors. No competitor provides this with the same depth.

**Pick tracking and accountability** — Action Network's ability to track your picks over time with win/loss records, ROI, and bet sizing creates accountability that no other app provides. This feature set is the product's strongest moat.

---

## 4. Bleacher Report

### What They Get Wrong

**4.1 Algorithmically generated "hype" drowns out information**
Bleacher Report's home feed prioritizes content that generates engagement (hot takes, reaction pieces, highlight videos) over informational content (scores, standings, injury reports). The result is that a user who opens the app to check if a game is happening tonight must scroll past multiple reaction-bait headlines before finding schedule information.

**4.2 Score cards are visually noisy**
Bleacher Report's score cards include team logos, score, game status, a "trending" indicator, and frequently an inline video highlight or gif — all within the same card component. The visual weight is spread across too many elements for the eye to know where to go. Score legibility suffers because it competes with animation.

**4.3 Push notifications are the app's primary engagement mechanism and are over-deployed**
Bleacher Report sends notifications at extremely high frequency — score updates, trending stories, team-specific news, league news — with inadequate user controls. The settings page offers sport-level notification toggles but no granularity (e.g., "only notify me for final scores" or "only notify me for my teams"). Users either accept everything or turn off notifications entirely. This is a false binary.

**4.4 Odds integration is via sponsored placements, not product design**
Bleacher Report surfaces odds through what are effectively native advertising units — "BetMGM Odds" cards that appear in the feed. These are visually styled to look like editorial content but link out to a sportsbook. Users who want genuine odds context receive a commercial pitch instead. Trust erosion is significant.

**4.5 Video autoplay in score feeds**
Bleacher Report autoplays video highlights in score feeds. On cellular connections this creates data drain without user consent. In a quiet environment (office, library) the audio playback is actively embarrassing. Despite years of user complaints, this pattern persists because autoplay drives completion metrics.

### What They Get Right

**Team-centric personalization surface** — Bleacher Report's "My Teams" section (when set up) creates a genuinely useful single-screen summary: your team's next game, last game score, recent news, top story. The concept of a team-centric home screen rather than a league/date-centric one is the right mental model for most sports fans.

**Highlight integration with scores** — When a game ends, Bleacher Report links the final score card directly to the best highlights of the game within minutes. The workflow from "game ended → I want to see what happened" is shorter than any competitor. For users who watch games on delay, this is indispensable.

**Breaking news speed** — Bleacher Report consistently leads on breaking team news (trades, injuries, signings). The combination of real-time alerts and score context means that when a star player is scratched, the user can see both the news and the immediate line movement implication in adjacent cards.

---

## 5. Sofascore

### What They Get Wrong

**5.1 UI density is maximized to the point of unusability for casual users**
Sofascore is built by and for obsessive data consumers. A standard match card can contain: score, xG, possession, shots on target, corners, cards, momentum bar, odds, and head-to-head record — all simultaneously. On a 375px-wide phone screen, this is a pixel-dense wall of information. For casual fans, this is overwhelming. The app offers no "simple view" toggle.

**5.2 Navigation is sport-first, not personalization-first**
Sofascore's navigation requires the user to select a sport, then a competition, then a matchday. There is a "Favorites" section but it is secondary in the navigation hierarchy. A user who follows the Premier League, NBA, and NFL must make three separate navigations to see their games. There is no unified "my games today" view that works well.

**5.3 Odds providers change without user notification**
Sofascore partners with regional sportsbooks to show odds and these partnerships change. A user in the US may see FanDuel odds one week and DraftKings odds the next with no explanation. Line values differ between books, creating confusion when a user sees a different number than what they saw yesterday.

**5.4 Momentum widgets are not explained**
Sofascore's "momentum" visualization (a timeline bar showing which team was dominant at which point in the match) is one of the most interesting score-adjacent features in the industry — but it has no legend, no tooltip, and no explanation anywhere in the UI. New users routinely do not understand what it represents.

**5.5 Post-match statistics are comprehensive but not narrative**
After a match, Sofascore provides 30+ statistics. These are presented as a flat list with no hierarchy indicating which stats were decisive or unusual. A team that won with 28% possession does not have that highlighted as notable — it sits at the same visual weight as their corner count. Data without narrative is encyclopedia, not insight.

### What They Get Right

**Live data depth and accuracy** — Sofascore's real-time data is best-in-class. Live xG updates, player ratings updated per-minute, and near-instant goal/card notifications are unmatched. The data pipeline for soccer in particular (their home sport) is more reliable and more comprehensive than ESPN, Action Network, or Bleacher Report.

**Player-level granularity within score cards** — Sofascore surfaces individual player performance ratings (0–10 scale) on the score card without requiring a drill-down. This allows a user to immediately understand *who* drove the result, not just the final scoreline.

**Head-to-head historical context** — The H2H section in Sofascore's game detail view shows the last 10 meetings with scores, outcomes at each venue, and goal tallies. For games where historical matchups matter (rivalry games, playoff series), this is instantly valuable context.

**Global sport coverage breadth** — No app matches Sofascore for depth of coverage below Tier 1 sports. Uruguayan Primera División, Finnish Liiga hockey, Australian AFL — all covered with the same data depth as NFL. For the globally-minded fan, this is a genuine competitive moat.

## Implications for Scroll Down

### Things Scroll Down Explicitly Avoids (Validated by This Audit)

**1. Context collapse** — Every competitor shows scores as isolated data. Scroll Down's story-first scroll positions the score inside a narrative arc. The user understands not just what the score is but why it matters.

**2. Hard score/odds bifurcation** — The "Bet tab" pattern (ESPN, Bleacher Report) creates a two-class system. Scroll Down can surface odds inline with scores without requiring navigation.

**3. Notification as engagement hack** — Bleacher Report and ESPN use notifications to drive opens regardless of relevance. Scroll Down's notification model (only fire when there's something genuinely worth knowing for *this user's* preferences) avoids the boy-who-cried-wolf degradation.

**4. Information density without hierarchy** — Sofascore and Action Network give users everything simultaneously with no prioritization. Scroll Down's scroll metaphor enforces a natural hierarchy: the most important thing first, detail available on demand by scrolling deeper.

**5. Algorithmic hype injection** — Bleacher Report's feed pollutes signal with engagement-maximizing content. Scroll Down's model keeps the feed tethered to game reality (scores, lines, events) rather than reaction content.

### Things Scroll Down Should Match or Exceed

**1. ESPN's score recall speed and game state clarity** — The FINAL/LIVE/UPCOMING state communication and sub-second score load time are table stakes. Any perceptible latency on a score card destroys trust.

**2. The Athletic's editorial × score coexistence model** — The pinned score header above a narrative feed is the right pattern for live game coverage. The Athletic proves it works even at editorial scale.

**3. Action Network's line movement transparency** — Showing the line trajectory (open → current), not just the current number, tells a story. Scroll Down should surface this in a way that is legible to non-bettors (framing: "line has moved 2.5 points toward the Chiefs since open").

**4. Bleacher Report's team-centric personalization concept** — The "My Teams" view is the right mental model even if Bleacher Report executes it poorly. Scroll Down should offer a team-centric lens as first-class navigation, not an afterthought.

**5. Sofascore's player-level detail within score context** — Surfacing who scored, who assisted, or whose performance rating drove the result — without requiring a drill-down — collapses the "what happened?" question from a three-tap journey to a one-glance answer.

**6. The Athletic's post-game narrative speed** — The window between final whistle and first meaningful analysis is where fans are most engaged and least well-served. Being consistently fast in this window (< 10 minutes) is a defensible edge.

---

## Conclusion

The competitor landscape reveals a consistent blind spot: every major app treats scores as data points and treats narrative as a separate, downstream product. The design consequence is that users who want to understand *what's happening and why it matters* must context-switch between a score widget and an editorial surface. No single app closes this gap fluently.

Scroll Down's architectural bet — that the scroll is a narrative unit, and that scores, odds, and story belong in the same continuous surface — addresses the most universal failure in the category. The risk is execution: any perceptible lag in score freshness or any moment where the story feels disconnected from the live game state will cause users to default back to ESPN's scorestrip. The bar for data freshness and game state clarity must be ESPN-level or better. Everything above that bar is Scroll Down's to own.
